<reason>An elite, genuinely close debate decided at the fulcrum. B's route to victory rested on two claims in tension: that cash is shrinking and increasingly costly per transaction (so the mandate is a perpetual regressive tax), yet that market incentives guarantee acceptance will never collapse (so the mandate buys nothing). A converted that tension into the decisive attack: "You cannot spend four speeches explaining why rational retailers abandon cash and then promise they never will." B's holdout-equilibrium answer never reconciled rising per-transaction costs with a stable acceptance floor, and A also forced the concession that B would mandate after exclusion occurred — then won the timing frame ("a guarantee that arrives after the exclusion is not a guarantee; it is a condolence"). A additionally destroyed B's opening prepaid-card plank and answered the format dilemma head-on ("Yes, plainly... compliance and emptiness are opposites"). B fought back hard: the "tiny benefit or real cost" dilemma was the debate's best analytical move, the bill-acceptor/networked-till turn dented A's resilience plank, the regressive-premium and clerk-safety points survived, and B executed cleanly while both of A's rebuttals were clipped for length. That execution cost plus B's strong rebuttals keep the margin thin, but A answered the most important pressure more directly and closed with the clearer reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.6's demolition of the prepaid-card alternative — "CON's alternative to cash acceptance depends on cash acceptance," plus fees, ID thresholds, outage failure, and data trails — forced B to abandon its opening exclusion answer and retreat to EBT/basic accounts, reshaping the inclusion clash for the rest of the debate; A's closing then finished the job by exposing the contradiction between B's erosion analysis and its market-stability promise.</best_rebuttal>
